sections.title: Grammar
sections.html:
Read across. A reads from the left side. B answers from the right side. Choose one part from each column.

Grammar Box 1: Questions about now, the past, and the future (review)

QUESTION
What doyoudo on weekends?
What didyoudo last weekend?
What areyougoing to do this weekend?
→
ANSWER
Iusuallyplay soccer. / visit my family.
Iwatched / cleaneda movie. / the house.
I'mgoing torest. / cook for my family.

Grammar Box 2: Follow-up questions

SOMEONE SAYS
I got a new job.
My car broke down.
I went to a party.
I'm really tired today.
I like my neighborhood.
My week was busy. How was your week?
→
YOU ASK A FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
Really? Where? / That's great! When do you start?
Oh no! What happened? / Where is it now?
How was it? / Who did you go with?
Why? / Are you OK?
Why? / What do you like about it?
It was good, thanks. / What about you?

Grammar Box 3: Why…? → Because… (the reason)

QUESTION
Why doyoutake the bus?
Why doesshelike her job?
Why didyoustay home?
→
ANSWER
Becauseit's cheap. / I don't have a car.
Becausethe people are friendly. / it's near her home.
BecauseI was tired. / it was cold.

Grammar Box 4: …, so… (the result)

THE REASON
My car broke down,
It's only ten minutes away,
I was tired,
My job is far away,
→
THE RESULT
so I took the bus.
so I walk.
so I stayed home.
so I need a car.

Questions and answers

Q: What is a follow-up question?

A: A second question about the same topic. It shows you are listening and keeps the conversation going. I got a new job. → Really? Where?

Q: When do I use because?

A: Before the reason. I take the bus because it's cheap. The because part answers Why?

Q: When do I use so?

A: Before the result. It's cheap, so I take the bus. Put a comma before so.

Q: Can I use because and so in the same sentence?

A: No. Use one. ✓ I was tired, so I stayed home. ✓ I stayed home because I was tired.

Q: Can I start an answer with Because?

A: Yes, in a conversation, after Why?: Why? → Because I was tired. In writing, join it to the other sentence: I stayed home because I was tired.

Q: How do I ask the question back?

A: What about you? or And you? My week was busy. What about you?

Practice: Write because or so.

  1. I'm learning English ____________ I want a better job.
  2. It was raining, ____________ I took an umbrella.
  3. She likes her neighbors ____________ they are very friendly.
  4. The store was closed, ____________ we went home.
  5. He drinks coffee every morning ____________ he starts work at 6:00.
  6. My coworker was sick, ____________ I worked late.

Common mistakes

✗ Don't say✓ Say
Because I was tired, so I stayed home.I was tired, so I stayed home. / I stayed home because I was tired.
Why you take the bus?Why do you take the bus?
What you did last weekend?What did you do last weekend?
Because of it's cheap.Because it's cheap.
I going to rest.I'm going to rest.
(one word) "Good.""Good, thanks. I played soccer. What about you?"

Nota para hispanohablantes: En inglés, Why? (¿Por qué?) y because (porque) son dos palabras diferentes. So aquí significa «así que» o «por eso». No uses because y so en la misma oración: «Because I was tired, so I stayed home» está mal. Di: I was tired, so I stayed home. Y no olvides do / did en las preguntas: Why do you…? What did you…?

Tip for speakers of other languages: In English, a one-word answer can sound unfriendly or bored. Add a reason (because…) or ask a question back (What about you?).

lessons.teacher:
How to Use This Plan

You don't need to speak Spanish or any other language. Teach in English. Show, point, and gesture. Each Grammar page has one short Spanish note and one tip for speakers of other languages. Learners read them on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain them.

Instructions: use the same short task words every week: Listen. Circle. Check. Write. Work with a partner. Work in a group. Ask a follow-up question. The first student page lists them with a Spanish column and a "My language" column, so learners can look them up.

Instruction rule: Model it (do it with one learner while everyone watches), check it (ask: "Do you write or speak? How many questions?"), then go. Say less, show more.

Grouping toolkit: Pairs: turn to a neighbor; with an odd number, make one group of 3. Groups: 3–4 learners. Inside–outside circles: the inner circle faces out, the outer circle faces in; the outer circle moves one person to the right each round. Mingle: everyone stands and talks to many classmates. The teacher joins a pair only if one learner is left over.

When a learner is stuck or speaks another language to you: (1) show it: the picture, a gesture, or the board; (2) give one more short English example; (3) point to the grammar box on their page; (4) a classmate can help for a few seconds, then back to English. You don't need to understand what classmates say to each other.

Lesson 1 (Week 1): Tell Me More

At a glance

Objectives: learners can…

  • ask and answer questions about the present, the past, and the future in one conversation (review)
  • ask follow-up questions: Really? Why? What happened? How was it? What about you?
  • give a reason with because (I take the bus because it's cheap)
  • say a result with so (My car broke down, so I took the bus)
  • read a community center flyer and write 3 sentences about a classmate

Materials

  • name tags and markers
  • Student Pages for Lesson 1 (print for the number expected + 3 spares)
  • Talk Time question cards: cut up the cards on the Talk Time page (1 set per pair, or one set for each circle)
  • baseline snapshot checklist (after the answer key)
  • phone + small speaker, L3_L1_listening.mp3
  • Prep time: 25 min.

Key vocabulary (with pictures on the New Words page)

★ neighbor • ★ coworker • ★ small talk • ★ follow-up question • ★ reason • ★ good news • ★ bad news • ★ chat • ★ introduce • community center • volunteer • get along

Clock-time plan

Times are loose. If a step runs long, take time from Read & Write first, then from Talk Time.

TimeStepMinGrouping (15 / 7–8)If running behind
6:00–6:10Welcome + "One Question, One Follow-Up" (Week 1 opening)10Pairs (7 pairs + 1 trio / 3–4 pairs)One round only
6:10–6:15Orientation: How Our Class Works + Task Words5Whole classShow the times and say the 3 rules only
6:15–6:22New Words (picture page) + pair game7PairsTeach the ★ words only
6:22–6:34Listening: play 1 (Task A), play 2 (Tasks B and C) + "Say it"12Individuals, then pairs checkDo Task C together on the board
6:34–6:45Grammar Q&A: follow-ups, because, so + pair drill11Whole class, then pairsSkip the pair drill; Talk Time practices it
6:45–7:00BREAK15
7:00–7:12Talk Time: The Three-Question Rule + baseline snapshot12Two circles / one circleTwo rounds only
7:12–7:17Exit Ticket + Homework5IndividualsNever skip
7:17–7:25Read & Write: community center flyer + 3 sentences8Individuals, then pairsReading questions only; writing becomes homework
7:25–7:30Progress Check (first can-do self-check)5IndividualsDo it in Week 2 at 6:00, while people arrive

Skip order if you're running behind: (1) the Read & Write writing task (it becomes homework); (2) the pair drill at the end of Grammar; (3) half of Talk Time. Never skip: the listening tasks, the grammar boxes and the mistakes table, and the exit ticket.

Attendance (15 → 7–8): every step lists both sizes. With 5 or fewer, sit at one table: pair work stays in pairs, and circles become "rotate seats." Late arrivals join any pair or circle right away.

Step by step

Step 1 · 6:00–6:10 · Welcome + "One Question, One Follow-Up" · 10 min

  • Grouping: pairs. 15 learners: 7 pairs + 1 group of 3. 7–8 learners: 3–4 pairs. Learners write a first name on a name tag.
  • Before class: write on the board: What did you do last weekend? → Really? How was it?
  • Model with one learner: ask, "What did you do last weekend?" The learner answers. Then say, "Really? How was it?" Point to the second question on the board and say, "This is a follow-up question. It asks for more."
  • Do (round 1, 4 min): A asks one question from the board, B answers, A asks one follow-up. Switch.
  • Round 2 (4 min): new partner. Add a second question to the board: What are you going to do this weekend? → Why?
  • Late arrivals: join any pair as a group of 3.
  • If behind: one round only.

Step 2 · 6:10–6:15 · Orientation: How Our Class Works · 5 min

  • Grouping: whole class. Open the Student Pages to How Our Class Works.
  • Show the times: class 6:00, break 6:45, back 7:00, end 7:30.
  • The 3 rules (say and show): (1) "English in class. A classmate can help you for a few seconds. Then back to English." (2) "Homework every week. About 15 minutes." (3) "Phones are OK for the audio and a dictionary."
  • Task Words page: point to it. Say: "These are the words for our tasks. You can write them in your language here," and point to the My language column. No one has to.
  • Also say: "In this class, we don't give one-word answers. We give a reason, and we ask a question back."
  • If behind: show the times and say the 3 rules only.

Step 3 · 6:15–6:22 · New Words · 7 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the New Words page.
  • Do: point to each picture and say the word. Learners repeat once. Act out small talk (say "Nice day, isn't it?" to a learner), introduce (introduce one learner to another: "Rosa, this is Ana"), and get along (smile and shake hands with a learner).
  • Check meaning (1 min): ask, "Is your coworker at home or at work?" (at work) • "Is a new job good news or bad news?" (good news) • "Does a volunteer get money?" (no)
  • Pairs (2 min): A says a word; B points to the picture and makes a short sentence (My neighbor is friendly.). Switch.
  • My language column: learners may write each word in their language at home. Don't spend class time on it.
  • If behind: teach the ★ words only.

Step 4 · 6:22–6:34 · Listening + "Say it" · 12 min

  • Grouping: individuals, then pairs check.
  • Before you listen (1 min): say: "This is Elena. This is David. They're neighbors. They're at the laundromat. One person has good news. One person has bad news."
  • Play 1 → Task A (who has good news, who has bad news). Pairs compare. Check together.
  • Read Tasks B and C together (1 min) so learners know what to listen for.
  • Play 2 → Tasks B and C. Pairs compare. Then show the answers (answer key).
  • "Say it" (2 min): read 2 lines: "Really? Why?" and "What about you? How was your week?" The class repeats each line twice. Make Really? go up and sound interested.
  • The audio plays the conversation once (about 1:31). Press play again for play 2. A third play is fine if the class needs it.
  • If behind: do Task C together on the board, reading the lines yourself.

Step 5 · 6:34–6:45 · Grammar Q&A · 11 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the Grammar page. The left side is the question (or what someone says). The right side is the answer (or the follow-up).
  • Box 1 (review, 2 min): you read a question; the class answers from the right side. Point to the time words: on weekends (present), last weekend (past), this weekend (future). Don't re-teach; Level 2 taught these.
  • Box 2 (3 min): read a sentence from the left; the class reads a follow-up from the right. Then say your own news ("I have a new cat!") and wait for follow-ups.
  • Boxes 3 and 4 (3 min): write on the board: because + reason and so + result. Read one row from each box. Ask: "My car broke down. Is that the reason or the result?" (reason) "I took the bus." (result).
  • Check questions: "I stayed home ___ I was sick." (because) • "I was sick, ___ I stayed home." (so) • "Why ___ you take the bus?" (do)
  • Pair drill (last 3 min): A asks a Why…? question; B answers with because; A asks one follow-up. Switch.
  • If behind: skip the pair drill. Talk Time practices it.

Break · 6:45–7:00 · 15 min

  • Cut up or lay out the Talk Time question cards. Write on the board: Really? Why? What happened? How was it? What about you?

Step 6 · 7:00–7:12 · Talk Time: The Three-Question Rule · 12 min

  • Grouping: inside–outside circles. 15 learners: two circles of 7–8 (the teacher or one trio fills a gap). 7–8 learners: one circle. 5 or fewer: sit at one table and rotate seats.
  • The rule: the inner circle has a question card. A asks the card question. B answers. A must ask two follow-up questions. B must use because or so at least once. Then switch roles, and the outer circle moves one person to the right.
  • Model with one learner (1 min): "What do you do on weekends?" → "I play soccer." → "Really? Where?" → "In the park, because it's free." → "Who do you play with?"
  • Do: 3–4 rounds of about 2 minutes each. Learners write one answer on their Talk Time page after each round.
  • Baseline snapshot: while learners talk, the teacher (or a second volunteer) calls about 5 learners, one at a time, for 2 minutes and uses the checklist after the answer key. Do the rest in Weeks 2 and 3.
  • If behind: two rounds only.

Step 7 · 7:12–7:17 · Exit Ticket + Homework · 5 min · NEVER SKIP

  • Exit ticket: each learner writes two sentences on a slip: one about a classmate (Rosa takes the bus because she doesn't have a car.) and one with so. Collect at the door.
  • Homework: open the Homework page. Do item 1 together. Say: "About 15 minutes. Bring it next week."

Read & Write · 7:17–7:25 · A Community Center Flyer · 8 min

  • Grouping: individuals, then pairs check.
  • Read (3 min): learners read the flyer on the Read & Write page on their own and answer questions 1–5. Say: "Read fast first. Then find the answers."
  • Pairs check (2 min): compare answers; check together.
  • Write (3 min): learners write 3 sentences about a classmate from Talk Time, using the frame. One sentence needs because.
  • If behind: questions 1–5 only; the writing becomes homework.

Progress Check · 7:25–7:30 · First can-do self-check · 5 min

  • Grouping: individuals. Open the Progress Check page.
  • Part A: read the 4 sentences in the answer key, slowly, 2 times each. Learners circle the best follow-up.
  • Parts B and C: learners do them alone. Walk around and help with the instructions only.
  • Part D: read each "I can…" line aloud and point to the 3 faces: 😀 "I can do it." 🙂 "With a little help." 😐 "Not yet."
  • Collect the pages (or check them at the start of Week 2).
  • If behind: do the Progress Check in Week 2 at 6:00, while learners arrive.

Listening script: L3_L1_listening.mp3 (about 1:31; the conversation plays once, so press play again for the second listen)

Audio: play from a phone + small speaker. No speaker? Read the script with a volunteer, at a normal, friendly speed.

Narrator: Lesson one. Listening. Elena and David are neighbors. It's Saturday morning, and they're at the laundromat. Listen.

Elena: Hi, David! How are you?

David: Hi, Elena. I'm OK, thanks. I'm just really tired.

Elena: Really? Why?

David: Because my car broke down on Tuesday.

Elena: Oh no! What happened?

David: It just stopped on the highway. Now it's at the mechanic, so I took the bus to work every day this week.

Elena: That's bad news. When is it going to be ready?

David: Maybe next Friday. What about you? How was your week?

Elena: It was great! I have good news. I got a new job.

David: That's wonderful! Where is it?

Elena: At the hospital on Pine Street. I'm going to work in the kitchen.

David: Do you like it?

Elena: Yes, I love it, because the people are really friendly.

David: How do you get there?

Elena: I walk. It's only ten minutes from my apartment, so I don't need a car.

David: Lucky you! I really need my car, because my job is far away.

Elena: Do you want a ride on Monday? I start at seven.

David: Thanks, but I start at six. I'm going to take the bus again.

Elena: OK. Good luck with your car!

David: Thanks. And congratulations on your new job!

Narrator: That's the end of the listening.

Answer key

  • Listening Task A: 1 Elena, 2 David, 3 David, 4 Elena.
  • Listening Task B: 1 T, 2 F (he took the bus), 3 T, 4 F (at a hospital), 5 T, 6 F (he starts at six).
  • Listening Task C: 1 Because, 2 so, 3 because, 4 so, 5 because.
  • Grammar practice (because or so): 1 because, 2 so, 3 because, 4 so, 5 because, 6 so.
  • Read & Write: 1 Saturdays, 10:00–11:30 a.m. (Room 4) • 2 No. It's on Tuesdays and Thursdays. • 3 children (ages 6–12) • 4 set up chairs and welcome new families • 5 Sunday.
  • Progress Check Part A (the teacher says, 2 times each): 1 "I'm really tired today." → a (Why?) • 2 "I went to a wedding on Saturday." → b (How was it?) • 3 "I have good news!" → a (Really? What is it?) • 4 "My phone is broken." → b (Oh no! What happened?)
  • Progress Check Part B: 1 because, 2 so, 3 so, 4 because.
  • Progress Check Part C: any good follow-up question, for example 1 Really? Where? / When do you start? 2 How was it? / Who did you go with?
  • Progress Check scoring: A /4 + B /4 + C /2 = /10. This is not a test grade. It shows who needs more help with follow-ups (A, C) and with because / so (B).

Baseline snapshot checklist (Weeks 1–3)

Ask the 6 prompts, in this order. Check ✓ if the learner answers in a full sentence without help. Write ~ if they answer with help. Write + if they also add a reason or a detail. Leave it empty if not yet. The final exam uses the same prompts.

LearnerTell me about your week.What did you do last weekend?What are you going to do next month?Describe a friend.What was your life like as a child?What will you do if it rains on Saturday?





Prompts 4–6 use Lessons 2, 3, and 6 grammar. In Week 1, most learners can't answer them well yet. That is expected: they show growth at the final.

Teacher notes

  • Privacy: learners choose what to share. Any answer can be invented. Never ask about immigration status, money, or a real address. "I don't want to say" is always OK, and so is changing the topic.
  • Why follow-ups matter: at Level 2, learners answered questions. At Level 3, they keep the conversation going. Praise every follow-up you hear in Talk Time, even a simple Really?
  • because vs. so: because comes before the reason; so comes before the result. A quick test: "Why?" is answered by the because part.
  • Mixed levels: stronger learners ask three follow-ups instead of two and answer with two reasons. Learners who are new to the class use Box 2 on their page as a script.
  • New learners who skipped Level 2: pair them with a returning learner in Step 1 and Talk Time. Check the placement questions in the scope and sequence (Section 2.1) after class.
  • Typical mistakes this week: Because I was tired, so I stayed home (both words), Why you take the bus? (no do), What you did last weekend? (no did before the person), and one-word answers. Say the right form clearly; the learner repeats. Learners can read the Spanish note and the tip on their Grammar page themselves; you don't need to explain them.

sections.title: Grammar
sections.html:
Read across. A reads from the left side. B answers from the right side. Choose one part from each column.

Grammar Box 1: What does he look like? (looks)

QUESTION
What doeshe / shelook like?
What dotheylook like?
→
ANSWER
He's / She'stall. / short.
He has / She hasa beard. / glasses. / curly hair. / long, straight hair.
They'retall. / short.
They haveglasses. / short hair.

Grammar Box 2: What's he like? (personality)

QUESTION
What'she / shelike?
What aretheylike?
Isyour boss / your teachernice?
→
ANSWER
He's / She'sfriendly and funny. / quiet but hardworking. / very patient.
They'rereally friendly. / a little shy.
Yes, very nice. / Yes, really nice.He's very kind. / She's very patient.

Grammar Box 3: Which one is…? → The… with…

QUESTION
Which one is your sister?
Which one is Kevin?
Which one is your boss?
→
ANSWER
The woman with long hair. / She's the woman with glasses.
The tall man with a beard. / The man next to Sam.
The short man with curly hair. / The woman in the red shirt.

Grammar Box 4: Object pronouns: me, him, her, us, them

BEFORE THE VERB
I work here.
You are new.
He is friendly.
She is patient.
We are new.
They are funny.
→
AFTER THE VERB (or after with, to, for)
meMy coworker always helps me.
youCan I help you?
himAsk him for help.
herI work with her.
usLinda trains us on Mondays.
themI like them a lot.

Grammar Box 5: Questions and answers with object pronouns

QUESTION
Do you know Ana?
Do you know Mr. Lee?
Do you like your coworkers?
Can you call us later?
→
ANSWER
Yes, I work with her. She always helps me.
Yes, I see him every day. He's our neighbor.
Yes, I like them a lot. They're very friendly.
Sure. I can call you at 6:00.

Questions and answers

Q: What's the difference between What does she look like? and What's she like?

A: look like asks about looks: height, hair, glasses, clothes. She's tall. She has glasses. be like asks about personality: She's friendly and patient.

Q: Do I say hair or hairs?

A: hair (no -s) for the hair on your head: She has long, curly hair.

Q: Where does the describing word go?

A: Before the noun, and it never takes -s: a tall man, two tall men, curly hair. Or after be: He's tall.

Q: How do I say which person?

A: the + person + with + thing: the woman with glasses, the man with a beard. For clothes you can also say in: the man in the blue shirt.

Q: When do I use me, him, her, us, them?

A: After a verb (I know her) and after small words like with, to, for, at (Come with me. Talk to him.). Before the verb, use I, he, she, we, they.

Q: Can I compare two people?

A: Yes (Level 2): She's taller than me. He's funnier than his brother. Use me, not I, after than in conversation.

Q: Are there words I shouldn't use?

A: Yes. Talk about hair, height, glasses, beards, clothes, and personality. Words about a person's weight, skin color, or age can be rude.

Practice A: Write me, him, her, it, us, or them.

  1. Ana is my neighbor. I see ____________ every day.
  2. My brothers are very funny. I love ____________.
  3. Mr. Silva is patient. Ask ____________ for help.
  4. We're new here. Can you help ____________?
  5. I'm a little shy. Please talk to ____________ slowly.
  6. That's my phone. Can you give ____________ to me?

Practice B: Write look like or like.

  1. What does your brother ____________? He's tall, and he has a beard.
  2. What's your teacher ____________? She's very patient.
  3. What are your neighbors ____________? They're friendly.
  4. What does she ____________? She has curly hair and glasses.

Common mistakes

✗ Don't say✓ Say
She has long hairs.She has long hair.
What does she like? (about personality)What's she like? / What does she look like?
He is a man very tall.He's a very tall man. / He's very tall.
two talls mentwo tall men
Do you know Ana? Yes, I know.Yes, I know her.
I work with she.I work with her.
He help me every day.He helps me every day.

Nota para hispanohablantes: What's he like? = ¿Cómo es? (su personalidad). What does he look like? = ¿Cómo es físicamente? En inglés se dice hair sin -s: She has long hair (no hairs). Los adjetivos van antes del sustantivo y nunca llevan -s: two tall men. Después del verbo usa me, him, her, us, them: I know her (no I know she).

Tip for speakers of other languages: many verbs in English need an object word after them: I know her (not I know). Can you help me? (not Can you help? when you mean yourself).

lessons.teacher:
How to Use This Plan

You don't need to speak Spanish or any other language. Teach in English. Show, point, and gesture. Each Grammar page has one short Spanish note and one tip for speakers of other languages. Learners read them on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain them.

Instructions: use the same short task words every week: Listen. Circle. Check. Write. Work with a partner. Work in a group. Ask a follow-up question. Learners have the Task Words page from Lesson 1.

Instruction rule: Model it (do it with one learner while everyone watches), check it (ask: "Do you write or speak? Who talks first?"), then go. Say less, show more.

Grouping toolkit: Pairs: turn to a neighbor; with an odd number, make one group of 3. Groups: 3–4 learners. Inside–outside circles: the inner circle faces out, the outer circle faces in; the outer circle moves one person to the right each round. Mingle: everyone stands and talks to many classmates. The teacher joins a pair only if one learner is left over.

When a learner is stuck or speaks another language to you: (1) show it: the picture, a gesture, or the board; (2) give one more short English example; (3) point to the grammar box on their page; (4) a classmate can help for a few seconds, then back to English. You don't need to understand what classmates say to each other.

Lesson 2 (Week 2): Who's Who?

At a glance

Objectives: learners can…

  • describe how someone looks: height, hair, a beard, glasses, clothes (She's tall. She has curly hair.)
  • describe someone's personality (He's friendly and funny.)
  • ask and answer What does he look like? and What's he like?
  • pick someone out: Which one is your sister? → The woman with long hair.
  • use the object pronouns me, him, her, us, them (I work with her. She always helps me.)
  • read a short welcome email and write 3–4 sentences about a friend or family member

Materials

  • Student Pages for Lesson 2 (print for the number expected + 3 spares)
  • Talk Time: the crowd picture page (1 per learner) and the person cards (cut up; 1 set of A cards and 1 set of B cards per pair)
  • phone + small speaker, L3_L2_listening.mp3
  • the Lesson 1 baseline snapshot checklist (continue it this week)
  • Prep time: 20 min.

Key vocabulary (with pictures on the New Words page)

★ tall • ★ short • ★ curly hair • ★ straight hair • ★ beard • ★ glasses • ★ friendly • ★ shy • ★ funny • ★ hardworking • patient • quiet

Clock-time plan

Times are loose. If a step runs long, take time from Read & Write first, then from Talk Time.

TimeStepMinGrouping (15 / 7–8)If running behind
6:00–6:10Opening Talk + Homework Check10Pairs (7 pairs + 1 trio / 3–4 pairs)One card only
6:10–6:18New Words (picture page) + pair game8Whole class, then pairsTeach the ★ words only
6:18–6:30Listening: play 1 (Task A), play 2 (Tasks B and C) + "Say it"12Individuals, then pairs checkDo Task C together on the board
6:30–6:45Grammar Q&A: look like / be like, the… with…, object pronouns + pair drill15Whole class, then pairsSkip the pair drill; Talk Time practices it
6:45–7:00BREAK15
7:00–7:12Talk Time: Pick Them Up (information gap) + baseline snapshot12Pairs, then groups of 3Round 1 only
7:12–7:17Exit Ticket + Homework5IndividualsNever skip
7:17–7:25Read & Write: a welcome email + 3–4 sentences8Individuals, then pairsReading questions only; writing becomes homework
7:25–7:30Progress Check5IndividualsDo it in Week 3 at 6:00, while people arrive

Skip order if you're running behind: (1) the Read & Write writing task (it becomes homework); (2) the pair drill at the end of Grammar; (3) half of Talk Time. Never skip: the listening tasks, the grammar boxes and the mistakes table, and the exit ticket.

Attendance (15 → 7–8): every step lists both sizes. With 5 or fewer, sit at one table: pair work stays in pairs, and the groups of 3 become one group. Late arrivals join any pair right away.

Step by step

Step 1 · 6:00–6:10 · Opening Talk + Homework Check · 10 min

  • Grouping: pairs, the same partner for both parts. 15 learners: 7 pairs + 1 group of 3. 7–8 learners: 3–4 pairs.
  • Before class: write on the board: Ask one follow-up question. Give a reason: because… / so…
  • Opening Talk (6 min): learners open the Opening Talk page. A asks a card question; B answers with a reason; A asks one follow-up. Switch after each card.
  • Model with one learner: "Why are you learning English?" → (answer) → "Really? Where do you use English?"
  • Homework Check (4 min): partners compare Lesson 1 Homework item 1 (the because answers). Walk around. Write 2 common errors on the board and correct them together. Correct only those 2.
  • Late arrivals: join any pair as a group of 3.
  • If behind: one card only, then the homework check.

Step 2 · 6:10–6:18 · New Words · 8 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the New Words page.
  • Do: point to each picture and say the word. Learners repeat once. Use the class: "Who has glasses?" (learners with glasses raise a hand) • "Who has curly hair?" Act out shy (look down, speak very quietly: "…hi") and patient (wait calmly, smile, look at your watch).
  • Check meaning (1 min): "Is a beard on your head or on your face?" (face) • "A shy person talks a lot: yes or no?" (no) • "A hardworking person works a little or a lot?" (a lot)
  • Two groups of words: draw two columns on the board: LOOKS (tall, short, curly hair, straight hair, beard, glasses) and PERSONALITY (friendly, shy, funny, hardworking, patient, quiet). Learners say which column each word goes in.
  • Pairs (2 min): A says a word; B points to the picture and makes a sentence (My brother is tall. / My teacher is patient.). Switch.
  • If behind: teach the ★ words only.

Step 3 · 6:18–6:30 · Listening + "Say it" · 12 min

  • Grouping: individuals, then pairs check.
  • Before you listen (1 min): point to the picture on the Listening page. Say: "It's Omar's first day at a hotel. His supervisor is Linda. She tells him about two coworkers, Kevin and Nora. Who is Kevin? Who is Nora? Listen."
  • Play 1 → Task A (write the letter of each person). Pairs compare. Check together.
  • Read Tasks B and C together (1 min) so learners know what to listen for.
  • Play 2 → Tasks B and C. Pairs compare. Then show the answers (answer key).
  • "Say it" (2 min): read the words in the "Say it" box. Clap on the strong part: FRIENDly, HARDworking, PAtient, CURly, GLASSes. The class repeats each word twice, then the line Everyone likes him.
  • The audio plays the conversation once (about 1:28). Press play again for play 2. A third play is fine if the class needs it.
  • If behind: do Task C together on the board, reading the lines yourself.

Step 4 · 6:30–6:45 · Grammar Q&A · 15 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the Grammar page. The left side is the question. The right side is the answer.
  • Boxes 1 and 2 (4 min): write on the board: look like = LOOKS and be like = PERSONALITY. Ask about a famous cartoon character or a picture on the New Words page: "What does he look like?" → "He's tall. He has a beard." "What's he like?" → "He's funny."
  • Box 3 (2 min): point to the picture on the Listening page. Ask: "Which one is Nora?" → "The short woman with long, straight hair." Learners ask about Kevin and Sam.
  • Box 4 (4 min): read the two columns: I → me, he → him, she → her, we → us, they → them. Say: "The second word comes after the verb or after with, to, for." Read each example; the class repeats.
  • Check questions: "Do you know Ana? Yes, I know ___." (her) • "Ask Kevin. Ask ___." (him) • "What does she look ___?" (like) • "She has long ___." (hair, not hairs)
  • Practice A and B (3 min): learners write, then pairs check. Go over the answers.
  • Pair drill (last 2 min): A names a person in the class (only names!); B describes how the person looks, and A asks What's he / she like? B answers only with kind words.
  • If behind: skip the pair drill. Talk Time practices it.

Break · 6:45–7:00 · 15 min

  • Lay out the crowd picture pages and the person cards (A cards in one pile, B cards in another). Write on the board: What does he / she look like? What's he / she like? Is that him / her?

Step 5 · 7:00–7:12 · Talk Time: Pick Them Up · 12 min

  • Grouping: pairs, then groups of 3. 15 learners: 7 pairs + 1 group of 3 (two people share the A cards). 7–8 learners: 3–4 pairs. 5 or fewer: one group; take turns describing.
  • Round 1 (7 min): each pair has the crowd picture (people 1–12) and two piles of cards. A takes an A card and doesn't show it. A says, "Can you pick up my cousin at the bus station?" B asks, "What does she look like?" A describes the person on the card (height, hair, glasses or a beard, the shirt color). B points and says the number. A says, "Yes, that's her!" or "No, she has glasses." Then B asks one follow-up: "What's she like?" A invents an answer. Switch: B takes a B card.
  • Model with one learner (1 min): use card A1 (person 7) and the model dialogue on the Talk Time page.
  • Round 2 (4 min): groups of 3. Each learner describes a person they admire (a family member, a friend, a teacher), personality only, with one reason (My aunt is very patient, because she never gets angry.). The others ask one follow-up question each.
  • Writing: after round 1, learners write 2 of the people they found in the table on the Talk Time page.
  • Baseline snapshot: while learners talk, call about 5 learners (the ones you didn't talk to in Week 1) for 2 minutes each and use the Lesson 1 baseline checklist.
  • If behind: round 1 only.

Step 6 · 7:12–7:17 · Exit Ticket + Homework · 5 min · NEVER SKIP

  • Exit ticket: each learner writes two sentences on a slip about a friend or family member: one about how the person looks and one about what the person is like, with because or so (My brother is funny, so everyone likes him.). Collect at the door.
  • Homework: open the Homework page. Do item 1 together (describe one person on the board with the class). Say: "About 15 minutes. Bring it next week."

Read & Write · 7:17–7:25 · A Welcome Email · 8 min

  • Grouping: individuals, then pairs check.
  • Read (3 min): learners read the email on the Read & Write page and answer questions 1–5. Say: "Read fast first. Then find the answers."
  • Pairs check (2 min): compare answers; check together.
  • Write (3 min): learners write 3–4 sentences about a friend or family member: how the person looks, what the person is like, and one reason (because).
  • If behind: questions 1–5 only; the writing becomes homework.

Progress Check · 7:25–7:30 · 5 min

  • Grouping: individuals. Open the Progress Check page.
  • Part A: read the 4 sentences in the answer key, slowly, 2 times each. Learners circle a or b.
  • Parts B and C: learners do them alone. Walk around and help with the instructions only.
  • Part D: read each "I can…" line aloud and point to the 3 faces: 😀 "I can do it." 🙂 "With a little help." 😐 "Not yet."
  • Collect the pages (or check them at the start of Week 3).
  • If behind: do the Progress Check in Week 3 at 6:00, while learners arrive.

Listening script: L3_L2_listening.mp3 (about 1:28; the conversation plays once, so press play again for the second listen)

Audio: play from a phone + small speaker. No speaker? Read the script with a volunteer, at a normal, friendly speed.

Narrator: Lesson two. Listening. It's Omar's first day at a hotel. His supervisor, Linda, tells him about two coworkers. Listen.

Linda: Welcome, Omar! Today you're going to work with Kevin and Nora.

Omar: Great. What's Kevin like?

Linda: He's very friendly, and he's really funny. Everyone likes him.

Omar: What does he look like?

Linda: He's tall, and he has a beard and glasses. You can ask him for help.

Omar: OK. And who is Nora?

Linda: Nora is the short woman with long, straight hair. She's a little shy.

Omar: Is she nice?

Linda: Yes. She's quiet, but she's really hardworking.

Omar: Does she talk a lot?

Linda: Not at first. Talk to her, and ask her questions. She's very patient.

Omar: Where can I find them?

Linda: They're in the laundry room. Come with me. I can introduce you to them.

Omar: Is that Kevin? The man with curly hair?

Linda: No, that's Sam. He works at the front desk. Kevin is the tall man next to him.

Omar: Oh, I see him. He's waving at us.

Linda: Let's go and say hi to him.

Narrator: That's the end of the listening.

Answer key

  • Listening Task A: Kevin a (tall, beard, glasses) • Nora b (short, long straight hair) • Sam c (curly hair). Person d is not in the conversation.
  • Listening Task B: 1 Kevin, 2 Kevin, 3 Nora, 4 Nora, 5 Nora, 6 Nora.
  • Listening Task C: 1 him, 2 her, her, 3 them, 4 them, 5 him.
  • Grammar Practice A: 1 her, 2 them, 3 him, 4 us, 5 me, 6 it.
  • Grammar Practice B: 1 look like, 2 like, 3 like, 4 look like.
  • Talk Time, Round 1 (the number B should point to): A1 Lisa = 7 (tall woman, long straight hair, glasses, blue shirt) • A2 Pedro = 8 (tall man, beard, glasses, green shirt) • A3 Ana = 9 (short woman, curly hair, yellow shirt) • A4 Tom = 6 (short man, curly hair, glasses, orange shirt) • B1 Julia = 1 (tall woman, curly hair, glasses, red shirt) • B2 Mr. Park = 2 (man with a beard, no glasses, blue shirt) • B3 Rosa = 11 (short woman, glasses, gray shirt) • B4 Leo = 10 (tall man, curly hair, red shirt). The personality answers are invented: answers will vary.
  • Talk Time table and Round 2: answers will vary.
  • Homework 1 and 3: answers will vary. Homework 2: 1 him, 2 them, 3 her, 4 us. Homework 4: 1 because, 2 so, 3 because.
  • Read & Write: 1 Ben • 2 She has curly hair and glasses. • 3 He's funny and very friendly. • 4 Monday at 8:00 a.m. • 5 Lucy • Writing (C): answers will vary.
  • Progress Check Part A (the teacher says, 2 times each): 1 "My brother is tall, and he has a beard." → a • 2 "My neighbor never gets angry. She's very patient." → b • 3 "Which one is your sister? The woman with curly hair." → a • 4 "What's your coworker like? He's funny and friendly." → b
  • Progress Check Part B: 1 look like, 2 him, 3 them, 4 us.
  • Progress Check Part C: answers will vary; for example 1 She's short, and she has long hair. 2 She's very friendly.
  • Progress Check scoring: A /4 + B /4 + C /2 = /10. This is not a test grade. It shows who needs more help with look like / be like (A, B1, C) and with object pronouns (B2–B4).

Teacher notes

  • Kind words only (important): describe only hair, height, glasses, beards, clothes, and personality. Never use words about weight, skin color, or age, and never as a joke. If a learner uses one, say the kind word: "We say tall / short / curly hair." The people in the pictures are invented.
  • Real classmates: in the pair drill, learners describe classmates only with the New Words. If a learner seems uncomfortable, describe people in the pictures instead.
  • look like vs. be like: the most useful check is the answer: if the answer is about the body or clothes, the question is What does she look like? If it's about personality, it's What's she like?
  • Object pronouns: they come after the verb (I know her) and after small words like with, to, for, at (Come with me. Look at him.). Learners often drop them (I know.) or use the subject form (I work with she).
  • hair: hair on the head has no -s: She has long hair. Adjectives never take -s: two tall men.
  • Mixed levels: stronger learners describe a person in the crowd with 4 details and add a comparison (She's taller than number 3). Newer learners use the model dialogue on the Talk Time page as a script.
  • Typical mistakes this week: She has long hairs, What does she like? (for personality), He is a man very tall, I know. (no object), I work with she, He help me. Say the right form clearly; the learner repeats. Learners can read the Spanish note and the tip on their Grammar page themselves; you don't need to explain them.

sections.title: Grammar
sections.html:
Read across. A reads from the left side. B answers from the right side. Choose one part from each column.

Grammar Box 1: What did you use to do?

QUESTION
What didyouuse to doafter school? / on weekends?
What didshe / heuse to doin the evening? / in the summer?
Where didyouuse tolive? / work?
→
ANSWER
I used tohelp on the farm. / play soccer. / do chores.
She used to / He used tolisten to the radio. / swim in the river.
I used tolive in a village. / work on a farm.

Grammar Box 2: Did you use to…? Short answers

QUESTION
Didyouuse towalk to school? / climb trees?
Didyour familyuse tohave a radio? / have a TV?
→
ANSWER
Yes,Idid.
No,Ididn't.
Yes,wedid.
No,wedidn't.

Grammar Box 3: Then and now

THEN (used to / didn't use to)
I used to write letters.
I didn't use to drink coffee.
We used to live in a village.
She used to be very shy.
→
NOW (simple present)
Now I send text messages.
Now I drink it every day.
Now we live in a city.
Now she's very friendly.

Grammar Box 4: A habit, one time, or now?

A HABIT IN THE PAST (many times)
I used to walk to school.
We used to eat dinner at 8:00.
→
ONE TIME IN THE PAST
One day I took the bus.‖Now I usually drive.
Last night we ate at 6:00.‖Now we usually eat at 7:00.

Questions and answers

Q: What does used to mean?

A: Something happened many times in the past, and it's not true now. I used to live on a farm (but now I live in a city).

Q: Does used to change for he or she?

A: No. I used to, she used to, they used to. Then use the base verb: She used to walk (not walked).

Q: When do I write use to (no -d)?

A: After did and didn't: Did you use to walk? I didn't use to drink coffee.

Q: Can I use used to for one time?

A: No. For one time, use the simple past: Last summer I went to the beach. (not I used to go)

Q: Can I use used to for now?

A: No. used to is only for the past. For now, say usually or every day: Now I usually take the bus.

Q: How do I say it?

A: used to and use to both sound like "yoos-tuh."

Practice A: Write used to, use to, or didn't use to.

  1. When I was a child, I ____________ climb trees every day.
  2. We had no TV. We ____________ watch TV at night.
  3. Did your grandparents ____________ have a farm?
  4. My mother ____________ make bread every morning.
  5. I ____________ like coffee, but now I love it!
  6. Did you ____________ write letters?

Practice B: A habit, one time, or now? Circle.

  1. I used to swim in the river. (a habit / one time / now)
  2. Last Sunday I went to the river. (a habit / one time / now)
  3. My father used to work on weekends. (a habit / one time / now)
  4. I usually send text messages. (a habit / one time / now)

Common mistakes

✗ Don't say✓ Say
I use to live on a farm. (the past)I used to live on a farm.
Did you used to walk to school?Did you use to walk to school?
I didn't used to drink coffee.I didn't use to drink coffee.
She used to walked to school.She used to walk to school.
I used to go to Texas last year.I went to Texas last year.
I use to take the bus now.Now I usually take the bus.

Nota para hispanohablantes: used to es como el imperfecto (-aba / -ía) o solía: I used to play = Jugaba / Solía jugar. Úsalo solo para el pasado. En preguntas y negativos se escribe use (sin -d): Did you use to…? I didn't use to… Para una sola vez usa el pasado simple: Ayer fui = Yesterday I went (no used to go).

Tip for speakers of other languages: used to is only for the past. For now, say I usually…. For one time in the past, use the simple past (I went, I saw).

lessons.teacher:
How to Use This Plan

You don't need to speak Spanish or any other language. Teach in English. Show, point, and gesture. Each Grammar page has one short Spanish note and one tip for speakers of other languages. Learners read them on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain them.

Instructions: use the same short task words every week: Listen. Circle. Check. Write. Work with a partner. Work in a group. Ask a follow-up question. Learners have the Task Words page from Lesson 1.

Instruction rule: Model it (do it with one learner while everyone watches), check it (ask: "Do you write or speak? How many people do you talk to?"), then go. Say less, show more.

Grouping toolkit: Pairs: turn to a neighbor; with an odd number, make one group of 3. Groups: 3–4 learners. Inside–outside circles: the inner circle faces out, the outer circle faces in; the outer circle moves one person to the right each round. Mingle: everyone stands and talks to many classmates. The teacher joins a pair only if one learner is left over.

When a learner is stuck or speaks another language to you: (1) show it: the picture, a gesture, or the board; (2) give one more short English example; (3) point to the grammar box on their page; (4) a classmate can help for a few seconds, then back to English. You don't need to understand what classmates say to each other.

Lesson 3 (Week 3): When I Was Young

At a glance

Objectives: learners can…

  • say what they used to do (I used to help on the farm.)
  • say what they didn't use to do (I didn't use to drink coffee.)
  • ask and answer Did you use to…? → Yes, I did. / No, I didn't.
  • compare then and now (I used to write letters. Now I send text messages.)
  • tell the difference between a past habit (used to), one time in the past (simple past), and now (simple present)
  • read a short memory story and write 4 sentences about then and now

Materials

  • Student Pages for Lesson 3 (print for the number expected + 3 spares)
  • Talk Time: the "Then and Now" mingle sheet (on the Talk Time page; 1 per learner)
  • phone + small speaker, L3_L3_listening.mp3
  • the Lesson 1 baseline snapshot checklist (finish it this week)
  • optional: an old object or a photo of an old radio or phone to show (not a family photo)
  • Prep time: 15 min.

Key vocabulary (with pictures on the New Words page)

★ childhood • ★ village • ★ farm • ★ river • ★ climb trees • ★ chores • ★ feed the animals • ★ radio • ★ letter (mail) • ★ landline phone • jump rope • then / now

Clock-time plan

Times are loose. If a step runs long, take time from Read & Write first, then from Talk Time.

TimeStepMinGrouping (15 / 7–8)If running behind
6:00–6:10Opening Talk + Homework Check10Pairs (7 pairs + 1 trio / 3–4 pairs)One card only
6:10–6:18New Words (picture page) + pair game8Whole class, then pairsTeach the ★ words only
6:18–6:30Listening: play 1 (Task A), play 2 (Tasks B and C) + "Say it"12Individuals, then pairs checkDo Task C together on the board
6:30–6:45Grammar Q&A: used to / didn't use to / Did you use to…? + pair drill15Whole class, then pairsSkip the pair drill; Talk Time practices it
6:45–7:00BREAK15
7:00–7:12Talk Time: Then and Now Mingle + groups of 3 + baseline snapshot12Mingle, then groups of 3Mingle only
7:12–7:17Exit Ticket + Homework5IndividualsNever skip
7:17–7:25Read & Write: a memory story + 4 sentences8Individuals, then pairsReading questions only; writing becomes homework
7:25–7:30Progress Check5IndividualsDo it in Week 4 at 6:00, while people arrive

Skip order if you're running behind: (1) the Read & Write writing task (it becomes homework); (2) the pair drill at the end of Grammar; (3) half of Talk Time. Never skip: the listening tasks, the grammar boxes and the mistakes table, and the exit ticket.

Attendance (15 → 7–8): every step lists both sizes. With 5 or fewer, sit at one table: the mingle becomes "ask everyone at the table," and the groups of 3 become one group. Late arrivals join the mingle right away.

Step by step

Step 1 · 6:00–6:10 · Opening Talk + Homework Check · 10 min

  • Grouping: pairs, the same partner for both parts. 15 learners: 7 pairs + 1 group of 3. 7–8 learners: 3–4 pairs.
  • Before class: write on the board: What does he / she look like? What's he / she like?
  • Opening Talk (6 min): learners open the Opening Talk page. A asks a card question; B answers with 2–3 sentences; A asks one follow-up. Switch after each card.
  • Model with one learner: "Tell me about your best friend. What's she like?" → (answer) → "Really? What does she look like?"
  • Homework Check (4 min): partners read their Lesson 2 Homework item 1 (the person they described) to each other. Walk around. Write 2 common errors on the board (often long hairs or What does she like?) and correct them together.
  • Late arrivals: join any pair as a group of 3.
  • If behind: one card only, then the homework check.

Step 2 · 6:10–6:18 · New Words · 8 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the New Words page.
  • Do: point to each picture and say the word. Learners repeat once. Act out climb trees (climb with your arms), jump rope (turn a rope and jump), and feed the animals (throw corn to chickens).
  • Then / now: point to the last picture. Say: "Then, people listened to the radio. Now, we use a phone." Make two columns on the board: THEN and NOW. Learners say where radio, letter, landline phone, text message go.
  • Check meaning (1 min): "Is a village big or small?" (small) • "Are chores fun or work?" (work: cleaning, cooking, washing) • "Is your childhood now or in the past?" (in the past)
  • Pairs (2 min): A says a word; B points to the picture and makes a sentence (My grandmother had a farm.). Switch.
  • If behind: teach the ★ words only.

Step 3 · 6:18–6:30 · Listening + "Say it" · 12 min

  • Grouping: individuals, then pairs check.
  • Before you listen (1 min): point to the old photo on the Listening page. Say: "This is Daniel. This is his mother, Teresa. They're looking at an old photo of Teresa's childhood. Where did she live? Listen."
  • Play 1 → Task A (then or now). Pairs compare. Check together.
  • Read Tasks B and C together (1 min) so learners know what to listen for.
  • Play 2 → Tasks B and C. Pairs compare. Then show the answers (answer key).
  • "Say it" (2 min): say: "used to sounds like yoos-tuh." Read the line in the "Say it" box, then Did you use to walk? and I didn't use to have a TV. The class repeats each line twice. Point out that used to and use to sound the same.
  • The audio plays the conversation once (about 1:15). Press play again for play 2. A third play is fine if the class needs it.
  • If behind: do Task C together on the board, reading the lines yourself.

Step 4 · 6:30–6:45 · Grammar Q&A · 15 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the Grammar page. The left side is the question. The right side is the answer.
  • Draw a timeline on the board: a long line with THEN on the left and NOW on the right. Draw many small marks on the THEN side and write: I used to walk to school (many times). On the NOW side write: Now I drive.
  • Box 1 (3 min): read a question from the left; the class answers from the right. Then ask learners: "What did you use to do after school?"
  • Box 2 (3 min): questions and short answers: Did you use to…? → Yes, I did. / No, I didn't. Point to use (no -d) after did and didn't.
  • Boxes 3 and 4 (3 min): read the THEN / NOW rows. Then read Box 4: a habit (used to), one time (went), now (usually).
  • Check questions: "I ___ live in a village." (used to) • "Did you ___ walk to school?" (use to) • "Last Saturday I ___ to the park." (went, one time) • "Now I ___ drive to work." (usually)
  • Practice A and B (3 min): learners write, then pairs check. Go over the answers.
  • Pair drill (last 2 min): A asks Did you use to…? with a word from the New Words page; B answers with a short answer and one more sentence. Switch.
  • If behind: skip the pair drill. Talk Time practices it.

Break · 6:45–7:00 · 15 min

  • Write on the board: Did you use to…? Yes, I did. / No, I didn't. and Where? Why? When? What about now?

Step 5 · 7:00–7:12 · Talk Time: Then and Now Mingle · 12 min

  • Grouping: mingle, then groups of 3. 15 learners: everyone stands. 7–8 learners: everyone stands. 5 or fewer: sit together and ask everyone.
  • Round 1, mingle (7 min): learners take the "Then and Now" sheet. They walk and ask one classmate one question (Did you use to have a radio?). If the answer is Yes, they write the name and ask one follow-up (Where? Why?), and write a short answer. If No, they say thank you and ask another person. Try to get a different name for each line.
  • Model with one learner (1 min): "Did you use to walk far to school?" → "Yes, I did." → "Really? How far?" → "About one hour." Write the name and "1 hour."
  • Round 2, groups of 3 (4 min): learners fill in 3 rows of the "My Then and Now Chart" (1 minute). Then each learner says 3 sentences comparing then and now (I used to live in a village. Now I live in a city. I didn't use to cook, but now I cook every day.). Listeners ask one follow-up each.
  • Baseline snapshot: while learners talk, finish the Lesson 1 baseline checklist with the last learners.
  • If behind: the mingle only.

Step 6 · 7:12–7:17 · Exit Ticket + Homework · 5 min · NEVER SKIP

  • Exit ticket: each learner writes two sentences on a slip: one with used to or didn't use to, and one about now with because or so (I used to walk to work. Now I take the bus because I live far away.). Collect at the door.
  • Homework: open the Homework page. Do item 1 together (one used to sentence on the board). Say: "About 15 minutes. Bring it next week."

Read & Write · 7:17–7:25 · A Memory Story · 8 min

  • Grouping: individuals, then pairs check.
  • Read (3 min): learners read the story on the Read & Write page and answer questions 1–5. Say: "Read fast first. Then find the answers."
  • Pairs check (2 min): compare answers; check together.
  • Write (3 min): learners write 4 sentences: 2 with used to (then) and 2 about now. Any place they used to live, or any job they used to have, is OK.
  • If behind: questions 1–5 only; the writing becomes homework.

Progress Check · 7:25–7:30 · 5 min

  • Grouping: individuals. Open the Progress Check page.
  • Part A: read the 4 sentences in the answer key, slowly, 2 times each. Learners check Then or Now.
  • Parts B and C: learners do them alone. Walk around and help with the instructions only.
  • Part D: read each "I can…" line aloud and point to the 3 faces: 😀 "I can do it." 🙂 "With a little help." 😐 "Not yet."
  • Collect the pages (or check them at the start of Week 4).
  • If behind: do the Progress Check in Week 4 at 6:00, while learners arrive.

Listening script: L3_L3_listening.mp3 (about 1:15; the conversation plays once, so press play again for the second listen)

Audio: play from a phone + small speaker. No speaker? Read the script with a volunteer, at a normal, friendly speed.

Narrator: Lesson three. Listening. Daniel and his mother, Teresa, are looking at an old photo. Listen.

Daniel: Mom, is this you in the photo?

Teresa: Yes! That's me with my sister. We used to live in a small village.

Daniel: Is that your house?

Teresa: Yes. We used to live on a farm near a river.

Daniel: Did you use to help on the farm?

Teresa: Yes, I did. Every morning, I used to feed the animals before school.

Daniel: Wow. Did you use to walk to school?

Teresa: Yes. It was far, so we used to walk for an hour.

Daniel: What did you do after school?

Teresa: We used to do our chores. Then we used to climb trees and swim in the river.

Daniel: Did you have a TV?

Teresa: No, we didn't use to have a TV. We used to listen to the radio at night.

Daniel: And did you have a phone?

Teresa: No. We used to write letters to my aunt in the city. Now I send you text messages every day!

Daniel: That's true. Life is really different now.

Narrator: That's the end of the listening.

Answer key

  • Listening Task A: 1 Then, 2 Then, 3 Now, 4 Then.
  • Listening Task B (check ✓): 1 ✓ feed the animals, 2 ✓ walk to school, 3 ✓ climb trees, 4 ✓ swim in the river, 5 ✗ watch TV, 6 ✓ listen to the radio, 7 ✓ write letters, 8 ✗ talk on a landline phone. (6 checks.)
  • Listening Task C: 1 used to, 2 use to, 3 used to, 4 use to, 5 use to, 6 used to.
  • Grammar Practice A: 1 used to, 2 didn't use to, 3 use to, 4 used to, 5 didn't use to, 6 use to.
  • Grammar Practice B: 1 a habit, 2 one time, 3 a habit, 4 now.
  • Talk Time: answers will vary.
  • Homework 1 and 3: answers will vary. Homework 2: 1 I used to play soccer. 2 She used to work at a hotel. 3 We didn't use to have a car. 4 Did you use to live in a village? Homework 4: answers will vary (one sentence about looks, one about personality).
  • Read & Write: 1 in a small village (near the mountains) • 2 She carried water / she used to carry water from the river. • 3 No. She didn't use to have shoes for school. (She walked to school without shoes.) • 4 In a city, in an apartment. • 5 a garden / her garden • Writing (C): answers will vary.
  • Progress Check Part A (the teacher says, 2 times each): 1 "I used to live with my grandparents." → Then • 2 "I usually take the bus to work." → Now • 3 "We didn't use to have a car." → Then • 4 "My children send me text messages." → Now
  • Progress Check Part B: 1 used to, 2 use to, 3 use to, 4 used to.
  • Progress Check Part C: answers will vary; for example 1 I used to live in a village. 2 Now I live in a big city.
  • Progress Check scoring: A /4 + B /4 + C /2 = /10. This is not a test grade. It shows who needs more help hearing then vs. now (A) and with used to / use to (B, C).

Teacher notes

  • Choice and comfort (important): learners choose what to share. Childhood can be hard for some people. "A place I used to live," "a job I used to have," or an invented story are always OK. Never ask why someone moved or left a country. "I don't want to say" is always OK.
  • What used to means: something that happened many times in the past and is not true now. If it happened one time, use the simple past (Last year I went to Texas).
  • used to vs. use to: after did and didn't, write use (no -d): Did you use to…? I didn't use to… They sound the same, so this is a spelling point. Don't spend a lot of time on it.
  • Now: for now, use the simple present with usually / every day: Now I usually drive. Learners sometimes say I use to drive for now; say "Now you usually drive."
  • Mixed levels: stronger learners add a reason to each then/now sentence (I used to walk, because we didn't have a car). Newer learners use Box 1 and Box 3 as a script in Talk Time.
  • Typical mistakes this week: I use to live… (for the past), Did you used to…?, I didn't used to…, I used to go to Texas last year (one time), I am used to play soccer. Say the right form clearly; the learner repeats. Learners can read the Spanish note and the tip on their Grammar page themselves; you don't need to explain them.

sections.title: Listening
sections.html:
Listen to Elena. She had a small car accident. Now she's calling Mark at her insurance company.

A. Listen. Circle the answer.

  1. Where did it happen? a. in a parking lot b. at the intersection of Oak Street and Second Avenue c. on the highway
  2. Was anyone hurt? Yes / No

B. Listen again. Put the events in order. Write 1–5.

OrderWhat happened?
____A police officer wrote a report.
____Elena was driving to work.
____The other car hit her car.
____Elena stopped at the red light.
____Elena called her insurance company.

C. Listen again. Write was, were, or wasn't.

  1. ____________ anyone hurt?
  2. What ____________ you doing when it happened?
  3. I ____________ driving to work.
  4. He ____________ talking on his phone.
  5. He ____________ looking, and he hit my car.
  6. Two people ____________ crossing the street.

Say it: I was driving. (wuz, short) • They were crossing. (wer, short) • Yes, I WAS. (strong)

sections.title: Grammar
sections.html:
Read across. A reads from the left side. B answers from the right side. Choose one part from each column.

Grammar Box 1: What were you doing?

QUESTION
What wereyoudoingat 8:00? / last night?
What weretheydoingat the corner?
What washe / shedoingin the parking lot?
→
ANSWER
I wasdriving / walkingto work. / home.
They werewaitingfor the bus. / at the light.
He was / She wascarryinga box. / some bags.

Grammar Box 2: Were you…? Was anyone…? Short answers

QUESTION
Wereyoudriving? / working?
Washe / shetalking on the phone?
Wasanyonehurt?
→
ANSWER
Yes,Iwas.
No,Iwasn't.
Yes,he / shewas.
No,he / shewasn't.
No,everyonewas OK.

Grammar Box 3: a long action + when + a short action

LONG ACTION (was / were + -ing)
I was waiting at the light
We were eating dinner
They were crossing the street
→
when
when‖a car hit my car.
when‖the phone rang.
when‖the light changed.

Grammar Box 4: while + a long action

While + LONG ACTION
While I was turning left,
While she was walking to work,
While we were waiting for the bus,
→
WHAT HAPPENED
the other driver was talking on the phone.
it started to rain.
we saw an accident.

Grammar Box 5: Review: should

QUESTION
What should I do?(after a small accident)
→
ANSWER
You shouldcall your insurance company. / take a picture. / tell your supervisor.
You shouldn'tleave. / get angry.

Questions and answers

Q: What does was / were + -ing mean?

A: An action was in progress at a time in the past. At 8:00 I was driving. (I started before 8:00 and stopped after 8:00.)

Q: was or were?

A: I / he / she / it was. you / we / they were. Negative: wasn't, weren't.

Q: Which action gets -ing?

A: The long action: I was waiting. The short action that happens in the middle is the simple past: a car hit my car (not was hitting).

Q: when or while?

A: while + the long action: While I was waiting… when + the short action: …when the phone rang.

Q: How do I say it?

A: In a sentence, was and were are short and quiet (wuz, wer). In short answers, they are strong: Yes, I was.

Practice A: Write was or were + the verb with -ing.

  1. At 7:00 I ____________________ (eat) breakfast.
  2. They ____________________ (wait) for the bus.
  3. ________ you ____________ (work) at 9:00 last night?
  4. She ____________________ (not / look) at the road.
  5. We ____________________ (watch) TV when the lights went out.
  6. What ________ he ____________ (do)?

Practice B: Circle the right words.

  1. I was driving when a car (hit / was hitting) my car.
  2. While I (cooked / was cooking), the phone rang.
  3. The phone (rang / was ringing) when I was taking a shower.
  4. I was sleeping (when / while) the alarm rang.
  5. (When / While) I was turning left, the other driver was talking on the phone.
  6. You (should / should to) call your insurance company.

Common mistakes

✗ Don't say✓ Say
I was drive to work.I was driving to work.
They was crossing the street.They were crossing the street.
I was waiting when a car was hitting my car.I was waiting when a car hit my car.
Were you work at 9:00?Were you working at 9:00?
While I cooking, the phone rang.While I was cooking, the phone rang.
You should to call the police.You should call the police.

Nota para hispanohablantes: I was driving = Estaba manejando. Usa was / were + -ing para la acción larga. La acción corta usa el pasado simple: when the phone rang = cuando sonó el teléfono (no was ringing). No olvides was / were: I was driving (no I driving).

Tip for speakers of other languages: long action = was / were + -ing. A short action that interrupts it = the simple past (hit, rang, saw).

lessons.teacher:
How to Use This Plan

You don't need to speak Spanish or any other language. Teach in English. Show, point, and gesture. Each Grammar page has one short Spanish note and one tip for speakers of other languages. Learners read them on their own. You never need to read, translate, or explain them.

Instructions: use the same short task words every week: Listen. Circle. Check. Write. Work with a partner. Work in a group. Ask a follow-up question. Learners have the Task Words page from Lesson 1.

Instruction rule: Model it (do it with one learner while everyone watches), check it (ask: "Do you write or speak? How many people do you talk to?"), then go. Say less, show more.

Grouping toolkit: Pairs: turn to a neighbor; with an odd number, make one group of 3. Groups: 3–4 learners. Inside–outside circles: the inner circle faces out, the outer circle faces in; the outer circle moves one person to the right each round. Mingle: everyone stands and talks to many classmates. The teacher joins a pair only if one learner is left over.

When a learner is stuck or speaks another language to you: (1) show it: the picture, a gesture, or the board; (2) give one more short English example; (3) point to the grammar box on their page; (4) a classmate can help for a few seconds, then back to English. You don't need to understand what classmates say to each other.

Lesson 4 (Week 4): It Happened So Fast

At a glance

Objectives: learners can…

  • say what they were doing at a time in the past (At 8:00 I was driving to work.)
  • ask and answer Were you…? → Yes, I was. / No, I wasn't. and Was anyone hurt?
  • tell what happened with when and while (I was waiting at the light when a car hit my car.)
  • answer an insurance agent's questions about a small car accident
  • describe what people were doing in a picture (a witness)
  • read a short accident story and fill out a simple accident report

Materials

  • Student Pages for Lesson 4 (print for the number expected + 3 spares)
  • Talk Time: the two pictures and the Witness Form (on the Talk Time pages)
  • phone + small speaker, L3_L4_listening.mp3
  • a phone with a timer (30 seconds for Talk Time)
  • optional: two toy cars to show hit and dent (or two books)
  • Prep time: 15 min.

Key vocabulary (with pictures on the New Words page)

★ accident • ★ intersection • ★ traffic light • ★ stop sign • ★ hit (a car) • ★ dent • ★ driver • ★ police officer • ★ witness • ★ insurance card • ★ report • wet floor

Clock-time plan

Times are loose. If a step runs long, take time from Read & Write first, then from Talk Time.

TimeStepMinGrouping (15 / 7–8)If running behind
6:00–6:10Opening Talk + Homework Check10Pairs (7 pairs + 1 trio / 3–4 pairs)One card only
6:10–6:18New Words (picture page) + pair game8Whole class, then pairsTeach the ★ words only
6:18–6:30Listening: play 1 (Task A), play 2 (Tasks B and C) + "Say it"12Individuals, then pairs checkDo Task C together on the board
6:30–6:45Grammar Q&A: was / were + -ing; when / while; should review + pair drill15Whole class, then pairsSkip the pair drill; Talk Time practices it
6:45–7:00BREAK15
7:00–7:12Talk Time: Witness (two pictures, a witness form)12PairsOne picture only
7:12–7:17Exit Ticket + Homework5IndividualsNever skip
7:17–7:25Read & Write: an accident story + an accident report8Individuals, then pairsReading questions only; the report becomes homework
7:25–7:30Progress Check5IndividualsDo it in Week 5 at 6:00, while people arrive

Skip order if you're running behind: (1) the Read & Write report (it becomes homework); (2) the pair drill at the end of Grammar; (3) half of Talk Time (one picture only). Never skip: the listening tasks, the grammar boxes and the mistakes table, and the exit ticket.

Attendance (15 → 7–8): every step lists both sizes. With 5 or fewer, sit at one table: Talk Time stays in pairs (or one group of 3, with two learners asking questions). Late arrivals join a pair as a second questioner.

Step by step

Step 1 · 6:00–6:10 · Opening Talk + Homework Check · 10 min

  • Grouping: pairs, the same partner for both parts. 15 learners: 7 pairs + 1 group of 3. 7–8 learners: 3–4 pairs.
  • Before class: write on the board: Did you use to…? What did you use to do?
  • Opening Talk (6 min): learners open the Opening Talk page. A asks a card question; B answers with 2–3 sentences; A asks one follow-up. Switch after each card.
  • Model with one learner: "Did you use to walk to school?" → (answer) → "Really? How far was it?"
  • Homework Check (4 min): partners read their Lesson 3 Homework item 1 (3 sentences about their childhood or a place they used to live) to each other. Walk around. Write 2 common errors on the board (often I use to live… or Did you used to…?) and correct them together.
  • Late arrivals: join any pair as a group of 3.
  • If behind: one card only, then the homework check.

Step 2 · 6:10–6:18 · New Words · 8 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the New Words page.
  • Do: point to each picture and say the word. Learners repeat once. Show hit and dent with two toy cars or two books: move one into the other ("hit"), then point to a small spot ("a dent, a small problem").
  • Keep it light: say "a small accident. No one is hurt. Only a dent." Use only the pictures; don't ask about learners' own accidents.
  • Check meaning (1 min): "Who saw the accident?" (a witness) • "Who writes the report?" (a police officer) • "Red light: stop or go?" (stop) • "Where do two streets meet?" (an intersection)
  • Pairs (2 min): A says a word; B points to the picture and makes a sentence (The driver stopped at the stop sign.). Switch.
  • If behind: teach the ★ words only. wet floor is for the workplace option (teacher notes).

Step 3 · 6:18–6:30 · Listening + "Say it" · 12 min

  • Grouping: individuals, then pairs check.
  • Before you listen (1 min): point to the accident picture on the New Words page. Say: "This is Elena's car. She had a small accident. No one was hurt. Now she's calling her insurance company. Where did it happen? Listen."
  • Play 1 → Task A (where? was anyone hurt?). Pairs compare. Check together.
  • Read Tasks B and C together (1 min) so learners know what to listen for.
  • Play 2 → Tasks B and C. Pairs compare. Then show the answers (answer key).
  • "Say it" (2 min): say: "In a sentence, was and were are short and quiet: I was driving (wuz). In a short answer, they're strong: Yes, I WAS." Read the lines in the "Say it" box. The class repeats each line twice.
  • The audio plays the conversation once (about 1:18). Press play again for play 2. A third play is fine if the class needs it.
  • If behind: do Task C together on the board, reading the lines yourself.

Step 4 · 6:30–6:45 · Grammar Q&A · 15 min

  • Grouping: whole class, then pairs. Show the Grammar page. The left side is the question. The right side is the answer.
  • Draw a timeline on the board: a long wavy line labeled I was driving (8:00–8:30) and a short arrow in the middle labeled a car hit my car (8:15). Say: "The long action is was + -ing. The short action is the simple past."
  • Box 1 (3 min): ask: "What were you doing at 8:00 this morning?" Learners answer: I was working. I was sleeping. Then read Box 1 across; the class answers from the right side.
  • Box 2 (2 min): questions and short answers: Were you driving? → Yes, I was. / No, I wasn't. Was anyone hurt? → No, everyone was OK.
  • Boxes 3 and 4 (4 min): when + the short action; while + the long action. Point to the timeline each time. Box 5 is a quick should review (You should take a picture.).
  • Check questions: "At 7:00 I ___ eating." (was) • "They ___ crossing the street." (were) • "I was cooking when the phone ___." (rang, a short action) • "___ I was walking home, it started to rain." (While)
  • Practice A and B (3 min): learners write, then pairs check. Go over the answers.
  • Pair drill (last 2 min): A says a time (Yesterday at 6:00?); B answers I was…ing. Switch.
  • If behind: skip the pair drill. Talk Time practices it.

Break · 6:45–7:00 · 15 min

  • Write on the board: What was he / she doing? He / She was…ing. Was anyone…? Yes, … was… / No, no one was…

Step 5 · 7:00–7:12 · Talk Time: Witness · 12 min

  • Grouping: pairs, A and B. 15 learners: 7 pairs + 1 group of 3 (two Bs ask questions). 7–8 learners: 3–4 pairs. 5 or fewer: pairs, or one group of 3.
  • Round 1 (5 min): A opens Picture 1 (Main Street). B does not look. Start the timer: A looks at the picture for 30 seconds and then turns the page over. B opens the Witness Form and asks the Round 1 questions (What was the man with the dog doing?). A answers from memory (He was walking.). B writes short answers.
  • Model with one learner (1 min): show Picture 1 to one learner for 30 seconds. Then ask: "Was anyone crossing the street?" → "Yes, a woman was crossing." Write it on the board.
  • Check (1 min): A and B look at the picture together. B checks ✓ the right answers.
  • Round 2 (5 min): switch. B looks at Picture 2 (the parking lot) for 30 seconds; A asks the Round 2 questions.
  • Fast pairs: add one question of their own (What was the man wearing?).
  • If behind: one picture only.

Step 6 · 7:12–7:17 · Exit Ticket + Homework · 5 min · NEVER SKIP

  • Exit ticket: each learner writes two sentences on a slip: one with was / were + -ing (At 7:00 last night I was cooking dinner.), and one with when or while and because or so (I was walking home when it started to rain, so I ran.). Collect at the door.
  • Homework: open the Homework page. Do item 1 together (one sentence on the board: Yesterday at 7:00 a.m., I was…). Say: "About 15 minutes. Bring it next week."

Read & Write · 7:17–7:25 · An Accident Story and Report · 8 min

  • Grouping: individuals, then pairs check.
  • Read (3 min): learners look at the 4-picture story and read Lee's story. Then they answer questions 1–5. Say: "Read fast first. Then find the answers."
  • Pairs check (1 min): compare answers; check together.
  • Write (4 min): learners fill out the Accident Report for Lee, with information from the story. Show where each answer is in the story (date, time, place).
  • If behind: questions 1–5 only; the report becomes homework.

Progress Check · 7:25–7:30 · 5 min

  • Grouping: individuals. Open the Progress Check page.
  • Part A: read the 4 sentences in the answer key, slowly, 2 times each. Learners circle a or b.
  • Parts B and C: learners do them alone. Walk around and help with the instructions only.
  • Part D: read each "I can…" line aloud and point to the 3 faces: 😀 "I can do it." 🙂 "With a little help." 😐 "Not yet."
  • Collect the pages (or check them at the start of Week 5).
  • If behind: do the Progress Check in Week 5 at 6:00, while learners arrive.

Listening script: L3_L4_listening.mp3 (about 1:18; the conversation plays once, so press play again for the second listen)

Audio: play from a phone + small speaker. No speaker? Read the script with a volunteer, at a normal, friendly speed.

Narrator: Lesson four. Listening. Elena had a small car accident. Now she's calling her insurance company. Listen.

Mark: Safe Road Insurance, this is Mark. How can I help you?

Elena: Hi, this is Elena Ramos. I had a small car accident this morning.

Mark: I'm sorry to hear that. Was anyone hurt?

Elena: No, everyone was OK. But my car has a dent.

Mark: Where did it happen?

Elena: At the intersection of Oak Street and Second Avenue.

Mark: What were you doing when it happened?

Elena: I was driving to work. The light was red, so I stopped.

Mark: And what was the other driver doing?

Elena: He was talking on his phone. He wasn't looking, and he hit my car.

Mark: Did anyone see the accident?

Elena: Yes. Two people were crossing the street. One woman gave me her phone number.

Mark: Good. Did the police come?

Elena: Yes. A police officer came and wrote a report.

Mark: OK. Please send me the report number today.

Elena: I will. Thank you for your help.

Narrator: That's the end of the listening.

Answer key

  • Listening Task A: 1 b (at the intersection of Oak Street and Second Avenue) • 2 No (everyone was OK).
  • Listening Task B (order): 1 Elena was driving to work. • 2 She stopped at the red light. • 3 The other car hit her car. • 4 A police officer wrote a report. • 5 Elena called her insurance company.
  • Listening Task C: 1 Was, 2 were, 3 was, 4 was, 5 wasn't, 6 were.
  • Grammar Practice A: 1 was eating, 2 were waiting, 3 Were … working, 4 wasn't looking, 5 were watching, 6 was … doing.
  • Grammar Practice B: 1 hit, 2 was cooking, 3 rang, 4 when, 5 While, 6 should.
  • Talk Time, Picture 1 (Main Street): 1 Yes. A woman was crossing the street. • 2 He was walking (with his dog). • 3 She was waiting for the bus. • 4 He was talking on the phone. • 5 She was eating ice cream. • 6 He was riding a bike.
  • Talk Time, Picture 2 (the parking lot): 1 She was shopping / pushing a shopping cart. • 2 He was carrying a box. • 3 Yes. A woman was running. • 4 He / She was drinking coffee. • 5 The blue car (at the top). • 6 answers will vary.
  • Homework 1, 3 and 4: answers will vary. Homework 2: 1 I was cooking when the phone rang. 2 We were watching TV when the lights went out. 3 She was walking to work when it started to rain. 4 They were eating dinner when their friend called.
  • Read & Write B: 1 He was driving to work. • 2 at the stop sign at Pine Street and River Road • 3 He was looking at his map (he wasn't looking at the road). • 4 No. No one was hurt. • 5 a man (who was) walking his dog
  • Read & Write C (sample report): Name: Lee Walker • Date: Tuesday, May 12 • Time: 8:10 a.m. • Place: Pine Street and River Road (at the stop sign) • What were you doing? I was waiting at the stop sign. / I was driving to work. • What happened? A truck hit my car from behind. • Was anyone hurt? No. • Damage: a dent • Witness: a man with a dog • Police report? Yes. Wording will vary.
  • Progress Check Part A (the teacher says, 2 times each): 1 "At eight o'clock this morning, I was driving to work." → a • 2 "She was waiting for the bus when it started to rain." → b • 3 "Was anyone hurt? No, everyone was OK." → b • 4 "The other driver was talking on the phone." → a
  • Progress Check Part B: 1 was, 2 were, 3 Were, 4 wasn't.
  • Progress Check Part C: answers will vary; for example 1 I was cooking dinner when my friend called. 2 While I was walking to work, I saw an accident.
  • Progress Check scoring: A /4 + B /4 + C /2 = /10. This is not a test grade. It shows who needs more help hearing the past continuous (A) and with was / were (B) and when / while (C).

Teacher notes

  • Keep it simple and non-graphic (important): this lesson is about dents, not injuries. Never ask about real accidents, injuries, or experiences with the police. Use the pictures and the invented stories. If a learner starts a personal story, thank them and go back to the picture. Say once, clearly: "In a real emergency, call 911."
  • Workplace option: if your class prefers, use a small workplace incident instead of the street pictures: I was carrying a box when I slipped on the wet floor. While I was mopping, a customer walked in. Use the wet floor card. The grammar is the same.
  • What the past continuous means: an action in progress at a time in the past (At 8:00 I was driving). It is often the "background" of a story; the short action that interrupts it is the simple past (when a car hit my car).
  • when or while: while goes with the long action (While I was waiting…); when usually goes with the short action (…when a car hit my car). Don't spend a long time on exceptions.
  • Mixed levels: stronger learners tell the whole picture story with when and while. Newer learners use Box 1 and Box 2 as a script in Talk Time.
  • Typical mistakes this week: I was drive, They was crossing, a car was hitting my car (for the short action), Were you work?, You should to call. Say the right form clearly; the learner repeats. Learners can read the Spanish note and the tip on their Grammar page themselves; you don't need to explain them.
